sections.heading: 3 EC-Bench
sections.text: We introduce EC-Bench, a benchmark for long-form quantitative video understanding. EC-Bench evaluates whether models can (i) identify the relevant set of countable instances , (ii) localize temporal evidence spans supporting those instances, and (iii) aggregate them into a correct numerical answer over extended temporal contexts. 3.1 Benchmark Design Tasks. EC-Bench comprises two tasks: Enumeration , which requires identifying and listing all query-relevant instances without omissions or duplicates, and Counting , which requires aggregating occurrences of those instances into a single numerical answer. Enumeration therefore evaluates whether a model correctly identifies the set of relevant instances before performing numerical aggregation. Evidence spans. For each query, we annotate one or multiple evidence spans , temporal sub-intervals that directly support the queried instances or their occurrences. In addition to producing an answer (a list for Enumeration and an integer for Counting), models are required to predict evidence spans on the original video timeline. This enables transparent inspection of model reasoning and facilitates interpretable evaluation. Reasoning categories. To capture diverse reasoning patterns in long-form videos, EC-Bench organizes queries into six reasoning categories. Fig. 2 provides representative Enumeration and Counting examples for each category. 3.2 Data Construction EC-Bench consists of 152 long-form videos, each exceeding 30 minutes in duration. The dataset is built upon LVBench [ 44 ] and expanded with additional sources across diverse domains, including sports, TV programs, documentaries, and online self-media. For each video, we construct both Enumeration and Counting queries, resulting in 1,699 open-ended queries. Multiple-choice formats are excluded to avoid answer biases and to better evaluate long-horizon reasoning with explicit evidence. Prompt design for QA generation. We design a structured prompt to generate high-quality Enumeration and Counting queries for long-form videos. The prompt instructs the model to analyze both visual and audio content over the entire video and generate queries spanning six reasoning categories. It further enforces that queries depend on full-video context, include explicit evidence spans, and follow standardized answer formats. To ensure consistency, we adopt a JSON-based output format and provide template examples across different video genres. Detailed prompts are provided in the supplementary material. Annotation and quality control. We adopt an annotation protocol inspired by prior long-video benchmarks [ 59 , 44 ] . We first generate initial query–answer pairs using Gemini-2.5-pro , followed by human verification. Annotators revise ambiguous or redundant queries, correct missing or misidentified instances, and refine evidence span boundaries to align with corresponding visual or audio events. Each sample is further cross-checked by another annotator to ensure consistency. Details of the annotation workflow are provided in the supplementary material. Figure 3 : Task statistics of EC-Bench. Top: reasoning category distribution for Enumeration (left) and Counting (right). Bottom: answer distributions for Enumeration (left) and Counting (right). 3.3 Dataset statistics EC-Bench covers diverse reasoning scenarios in long-form video understanding. Figure 3 and Figure 4 summarize the task-level and video-level statistics. Task statistics. Figure 3 summarizes the task-level statistics of EC-Bench. The top row shows the distribution of reasoning categories for Enumeration (left) and Counting (right). The dataset is intentionally balanced across six categories: Parallel, Causal, Speech/Audio, Appearance, Spatial, and Conditional. Each category accounts for approximately 16–17% of the queries. This balanced design helps ensure that EC-Bench evaluates diverse reasoning patterns rather than emphasizing a particular task type. The bottom row illustrates the answer distributions for the two tasks. For Enumeration, the number of listed instances is typically between 2 and 6 (mean: 5.32), with some cases exceeding ten items, encouraging models to achieve both coverage and consistency in instance identification. For Counting, numerical answers are concentrated between 1 and 8 while also including a smaller number of larger counts, enabling evaluation across both common and more challenging counting scenarios. Figure 4 : Video statistics of EC-Bench. Left: distribution of video durations (all videos exceed 30 minutes; median 47 minutes). Right: representative examples of video genres in the dataset. Video Statistics. Figure 4 presents the distribution of video durations and genres. All 152 videos exceed 30 minutes in length, with a median duration of 47 minutes and an average duration of approximately 57 minutes. The dataset spans diverse domains including documentaries (17%), Selfmedia (16%), Sports (18%), TV and Live (14% each), Cartoons (12%), News (7%), and Academic (2%). This diversity in both tasks and video sources allows EC-Bench to evaluate long-range temporal reasoning and quantitative understanding across varied video contexts. Figure 5 : Video length comparison with the existing dataset. Figure 5 highlights differences in video-length distributions between datasets. Videos in CG-AV-Counting [ 5 ] are largely concentrated within the 0–25 minute range, typically consisting of short clips centered on single events. In contrast, all videos in EC-Bench exceed 30 minutes, with a median duration of approximately 47 minutes. This difference suggests that EC-Bench introduces additional challenges compared with existing counting datasets. 3.4 Evaluation Metrics Enumeration. For Enumeration, we evaluate the quality of predicted item lists using precision, recall, and F1-score. To match predicted items with ground-truth annotations, we employ an external LLM-as-a-Judge procedure that classifies each predicted item as a True Positive (TP), False Positive (FP), or False Negative (FN). Precision ( T ​ P / ( T ​ P + F ​ P ) TP/(TP+FP) ), recall ( T ​ P / ( T ​ P + F ​ N ) TP/(TP+FN) ), and F1-score are computed from these classifications. We validate the LLM-as-Judge through a human study on 100 Enumeration queries, showing a strong correlation with human F1 scores (Spearman ρ = 0.8233 \rho=0.8233 , p < 0.0001 p<0.0001 ). Counting. For Counting, we report exact-match accuracy and Mean Absolute Error (MAE), as exact matching alone may be overly strict when the predicted count is close to the ground truth. Evidence spans. We evaluate temporal evidence grounding using temporal IoU (tIoU) between predicted and ground-truth evidence spans. When multiple spans are present, predicted spans are merged into a single interval P P , and ground-truth spans into a single interval G G . We then compute tIoU = | P ∩ G | / | P ∪ G | \mathrm{tIoU}=|P\cap G|/|P\cup G| . This metric reflects how accurately the model localizes the overall temporal evidence region. We report mean tIoU over all queries.

sections.heading: 4 Experiments
sections.text: We evaluate the performance of recent MLLMs on EC-Bench. Our experiments cover a diverse set of open-source and proprietary systems to assess current capabilities in long-form video reasoning. 4.1 Settings Open-source models. We evaluated several open-source models: LongLLaVA 9B [ 45 ] , LongVA DPO 7B [ 56 ] , VideoLLaMA3 2B [ 55 ] , VideoLLaMA3 7B [ 55 ] , LLaVA-Next-Video 7B [ 57 ] , LLaVA-Next-Video 34B [ 57 ] , InternVideo2.5 8B [ 46 ] , mPLUG-Owl3 7B [ 51 ] , VideoChat-Flash 7B [ 25 ] , MiMo-VL 7B RL [ 49 ] , LongVILA-R1 7B [ 7 ] , LLaVA-OneVision1.5 8B [ 1 ] , Qwen3-VL 8B [ 3 ] , Qwen3-VL 32B [ 3 ] , Vamba [ 38 ] , and InternVL3.5 38B [ 8 ] . These models represent recent open MLLMs designed for video understanding and long-context reasoning. Proprietary models. We additionally evaluated six proprietary models: GPT-4o [ 34 ] , GPT-4.1 [ 35 ] , GPT-5 [ 35 ] , Gemini 2.0 Flash [ 14 ] , Gemini 2.5 Flash [ 14 ] , and Gemini 2.5 Pro [ 14 ] . These models represent state-of-the-art commercial multimodal systems with strong long-context reasoning capabilities. Input configuration. To ensure fair comparison, we standardize the input format across all models. • Visual input. Video frames are uniformly sampled and provided as an image sequence. Sampling intervals are adjusted according to video duration to remain within each model’s maximum context length. • Temporal information. Each frame is paired with its timestamp, enabling models to reason over temporal order and long-range dependencies. • Audio input. Audio tracks are transcribed using Whisper-large-v3 [ 37 ] to produce timestamp-aligned transcripts used as textual input. • Prompt. A standardized instruction prompt specifies the task type (Enumeration or Counting) and requires models to report supporting evidence intervals for each answer. The full prompt specification is provided in the supplementary material. Output configuration. All models receive only the question text without multiple-choice options and are required to produce open-ended answers. Model outputs are normalized before evaluation by standardizing punctuation, letter case, and time expressions to ensure consistent matching with ground-truth annotations. Best and second-best results in each column are highlighted with darker and lighter shading, respectively. 4.2 Results Table 2 summarizes the quantitative performance of open-source and proprietary MLLMs on EC-Bench. We report accuracy for Enumeration and Counting, together with performance across six reasoning categories. To provide a reference for model performance, we conducted a human evaluation with balanced coverage across the six reasoning categories. Human performance reaches 78.57% on Enumeration and 82.97% on Counting. Proprietary vs. open-source models. Table 2 shows a clear performance gap between proprietary and open-source models across EC-Bench tasks. Proprietary models consistently occupy the top tier, with GPT and Gemini families achieving the highest overall scores in both Enumeration and Counting. In contrast, open-source models generally perform substantially worse, although some models achieve competitive results in simpler perception-oriented categories such as Parallel and Appearance. Performance differences become more pronounced in categories that require stronger reasoning over long temporal contexts. Both Enumeration and Counting show noticeable drops in tasks such as Causal and Conditional reasoning, suggesting that current models struggle to integrate evidence across distant temporal segments. This trend is consistent across both proprietary and open-source models. Human performance further highlights the difficulty of the benchmark. In our human evaluation, accuracy reaches 78.57% on Enumeration and 82.97% on Counting, substantially higher than the best model results. These findings suggest that long-form quantitative reasoning in videos, particularly identifying all relevant instances and aggregating them across time, remains a challenging problem for current multimodal models. (a) Enumeration. (b) Counting. Figure 6 : Enumeration and counting accuracy across video genres. Performance across video genres. Figure 6 compares model accuracy across eight video genres: Academic , Cartoon , Documentary , Live , News , Selfmedia , Sports , and TV . In the Enumeration task (Fig. 6(a) ), proprietary models such as GPT-5 and the Gemini family consistently outperform open-source models across most genres. Their performance remains relatively stable across domains, indicating strong ability to identify relevant instances in long videos. In the Counting task (Fig. 6(b) ), performance differences become more pronounced across genres. While proprietary models still achieve the best overall accuracy, all models show noticeable drops in several domains, suggesting that aggregating instances over long temporal contexts remains challenging. Overall, the results indicate that EC-Bench covers diverse video genres and reveals clear domain-dependent performance differences among current MLLMs. 4.3 Ablation Studies Effect of enumeration prompting. To investigate the impact of enumeration on counting, we introduce an explicit enumeration-first prompting strategy. In this setup, models are instructed to first enumerate relevant events before performing the counting step. The full prompt specification is provided in the supplementary material. Table 8(a) evaluates this strategy on two open-source and two proprietary models. As shown in Table 8(a) , enumeration-first prompting consistently improves counting accuracy and reduces MAE across all evaluated models. The gains are larger for open-source models, while proprietary models show smaller but consistent improvements. These results suggest that explicitly enumerating events before aggregation helps stabilize numerical reasoning in long-form videos and improves counting performance without additional model training. Effect of frame density. Fig. 8(b) analyzes the impact of input frame count on model performance. For Gemini-2.5-Flash, increasing the number of frames from 128 to 512 improves both Enumeration and Counting accuracy, indicating that broader temporal coverage helps reduce missed events. However, the gains diminish beyond this point and slightly decrease at higher frame counts, suggesting that simply increasing the number of frames introduces redundancy or noise without improving instance identification. A similar pattern is observed for Qwen3-VL 8B, where moderate frame increases provide small improvements but performance drops when too many frames are used. These results suggest that while additional frames can improve temporal coverage, naive increases in frame density do not consistently improve performance. Instead, performance is likely limited by the model’s ability to identify and integrate relevant instances over long temporal contexts. 4.4 Analysis We perform additional analysis to isolate the contributions of temporal coverage, visual domain differences, and model capacities. Correlation between enumeration and counting. Based on the results in Table 2 , we analyze the relationship between model performance on Enumeration and Counting. We observe a clear positive association (Spearman’s ρ = 0.692 \rho=0.692 ), indicating that models with higher enumeration accuracy also tend to achieve better counting performance. This result suggests that both tasks rely on shared underlying capabilities, such as maintaining temporal consistency and consistently identifying relevant instances across long video sequences. Figure 8 : Analysis of EC-Bench performance. Importance of Temporal Span Accuracy. Table 8(c) examines the relationship between temporal evidence localization and quantitative reasoning performance. In this evaluation, tIoU measures the overlap between predicted and ground-truth evidence spans associated with the queried events. The results indicate a clear correlation between temporal grounding quality and task performance. Models that achieve higher tIoU scores generally exhibit lower counting errors and higher enumeration precision and recall. Proprietary models such as GPT-5 and the Gemini family tend to achieve both stronger temporal localization and higher quantitative reasoning accuracy. In contrast, most open-source models obtain substantially lower tIoU scores, and their counting and enumeration accuracy is correspondingly weaker. These results suggest that accurately identifying the relevant temporal evidence spans plays an important role in improving quantitative reasoning performance in long-form videos. Failure Analysis. We analyze failure cases using GPT-4o, a representative multimodal model with competitive performance on EC-Bench. The analysis reveals several consistent failure patterns across both Enumeration and Counting tasks: - Undercounting in Crowded Scenes. In crowded scenes, the model often undercounts people or objects because it does not individuate each instance. For example, when asked “What is the maximum number of people trapped in capsules?”, the ground truth is 87 while GPT-4o outputs 3. - Audio-based Failure. For audio-based counting, the model frequently predicts numbers that match the general topic of the video rather than the actual number of occurrences, such as answering 5 instead of the correct 26 for “How many times is AI-generated content shown?”. - Abstraction in Enumeration. In Enumeration tasks, the model often replaces detailed lists with abstract categories, ignoring the requirement to list all items. A typical case is “List the technical terms for Changi Airport T4”, where specific items are replaced by broad labels such as “self-service systems”. - World-Knowledge Hallucination. For slide or timeline enumeration, the model sometimes hallucinates items based on world knowledge rather than visual evidence, such as generating NVIDIA-related terms for “List the items under ‘GENERATIVE AI’ at 6:54”. These patterns highlight systematic limitations in instance-level reasoning and evidence grounding in long-form videos.

sections.heading: 5 Discussion
sections.text: EC-Bench reveals that long-form video understanding remains a major challenge for current multimodal LLMs. Although proprietary systems such as GPT-5 and the Gemini family outperform open-source models, their absolute accuracy remains far below human performance. Our analysis suggests that the primary difficulty lies in temporal grounding rather than numerical aggregation itself. In long-form videos, models must first identify relevant instances and localize their supporting temporal evidence before aggregating them into a final count. The strong correlation between enumeration accuracy, temporal span localization, and counting performance supports this interpretation. Our ablation studies further reinforce this observation. Enumeration-first prompting consistently improves counting accuracy across models, indicating that explicitly structuring reasoning around instance identification can stabilize numerical reasoning. In contrast, increasing the number of input frames provides only limited improvements and quickly saturates, suggesting that naive scaling of temporal coverage alone does not address the underlying challenge. In summary, these findings highlight that accurate instance identification and temporal grounding are more critical than simply increasing input frame density. Progress in long-video quantitative reasoning will likely require models that explicitly reason over long temporal contexts and ground events in time, rather than relying on architectures designed for short-video settings.
